The reason you didn't see a terribly substantial change from 0-100 to 20-80 charge is twofold: 1: Battery engineers know about this effect already. The lithium's "true" 0 and 100% are not available to you, whether it's in a phone or an electric car or whatever. 2: The 40% reduction in discharge/charge allowance has already been enacted in the battery charge circuit in the phones. The rate of loss of charge capacity is logarithmic, the most substantial chunk of effective withheld depth of discharge has already been withheld from you. It's strikingly similar to how bearing lifetimes are calculated. Device power demands, battery size, and charge circuit design are all carefully balanced by engineers in order to produce what is considered to be a good balance of processing power, cost, weight, longevity, etc. Although you can totally gain more battery lifetime by reducing your depth of discharge, it is a rapidly diminishing return. You might as well just use the phone like normal and replace the battery when its capacity becomes unacceptable. Replacing a battery isn't terribly expensive in a phone. Regarding charge rate, I cannot remember the exact details of what was taught in my vehicle powertrains class. If i remember correctly, the primary issue you see with high speed charging has to do with heat buildup. An electric car, for example, is able to effectively dissipate a substantial amount of heat from the batteries during fast charging. On the other hand, a cell phone fast charging, particularly one sitting in the hot sun or perhaps running intensive software, will not. Therefore, the phone may either allow its battery to be degraded due to the heat buildup of the fast charging, or it may throttle the charging rate in order to manage heat buildup. At the end of the day, the single biggest factor for determining expected lithium battery lifetime is cumulative depth of discharge/charge. Limiting this as much as possible produces the most significant results, with the majority of the actually effective change coming from the first bit of DOD limitation.

- Fast charging does not significantly damage the battery. After 500 cycles, the difference is only about 0.3–0.5 percent compared to slow charging. - Keeping the battery between 30 and 80 percent helps a bit, but the effect is small, around 2–4 percent better. - Storing the phone fully charged at 100 percent for a week does not reduce capacity noticeably. - The main factor in battery wear is charge cycles, not charging speed. - Phone performance does not drop much with battery wear, but weaker batteries throttle earlier and reduce usage time. - Replace the battery when its health is around 80 to 85 percent. - Main takeaway: use any charger you like, just avoid overheating. No need to worry about fast charging.

videos.title: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Review - 4 Months Later
videos.description: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Review - 4 Months Later Buy Galaxy Z Fold 8 here - https://tinyurl.com/mrxy4ee2 When I first got my hands on the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, I was genuinely excited. The thinner design, the improved displays, the new hinge, and the fact that Samsung was finally taking this form factor in a slightly different direction made this feel like a pretty interesting upgrade. But that was four months ago. But what about now? Well, here's my review of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 after 4 months of using it everyday.

comments.text: People really underestimate how important pocketability is... as someone who rocked an s23 ultra for years, it was an amazing device but my god it was so unwieldy. Its so satisfying to to have a phone that you can fold up and that it actually fits firmly in your pocket instead of sticking out.

This is my first Samsung phone. I've been an iPhone user since the very first one back in 2007. I bought the iPhone Duo and hated the experience ended up returning it. Never in my wildest dream I saw myself owning a Samsung phone. While I do own a lot of apple products this phone here is amazing. The only thing I wish it had was a telephoto lens.

For me, the Fold 8—aside from the lack of a telephoto camera—is nearly perfect. In essence, it is exactly the device I have wished for ever since the very first Galaxy Fold. I still remember clearly when I first saw the original Fold at a Saturn electronics store. My first thought was: Why is the device so tall and narrow when closed? Why couldn’t it be a bit wider, with proportions more reminiscent of a classic BlackBerry? Even back then, it was clear to me that the gap between the two halves of the display would eventually have to close—which, as it turns out, is now the case. It’s truly fascinating how, over the years, the Fold has evolved closer and closer to what I had envisioned back then. With the Fold 8, that vision has now become almost a reality for me. Now, all that’s really missing is a proper telephoto camera and some customizing stuff from Samsung that is not in GoodLock (for now); if it had that, it would be the perfect smartphone for me.
I've owned the Fold 8 for a couple of months now. I love it. It's the best smart phone I have ever owned. I use it so much, that it has almost replaced my work laptop and personal tablet.

Terrific video. You really hit the key points and your side by side comparisons are exactly the way to do this. I'm an old professional photographer and I have an iPhone 17 (which I bought after my ex wife kicked my butt, my iPhone 12's butt and my Nikon D850s butt!! at our son's wedding.) I initially thought she might like to see this video... but she really doesn't need to. She's got a great phone that does what almost everyone wants a smart phone camera to do. And she paid a lot less for her Pixel. For the typical person, they're all really good cameras. As a pro I've spent decades learning to look for specific things. When I'm done with an image even my most visually adept clients can't tell the difference between 60% of what I did and the 100% I insist on. So a Pixel for a few $$ versus a >$2k iPhone Pro Max? Save the money and don't fear dropping or losing the less expensive phone. One thing that is going on with the Galaxy and the Pixel is they pump things up a bit. With action cameras trying to keep up with GoPro, they will say, and deliver the same pixel count, but clearly their sensors are half what the GoPro has; they've just double the pixel count of the image. It's math and a hustle but it's not detail or quality. I don't think the other two cameras are doing this, but they're doing some things. And the comment about the Pixel's moon? Is it real or.... If they can just insert exactly the phase, and anything in front of the moon? I guess, Why not? Except for shadows right at the edge, the moon has been exactly the same forever. For me though I can see the quality in the iPhone images, but I also know that this little bit of quality does a couple of things. First, the initial photo you get will tend to look flatter than the ones from the other phones. For a pro, no problem. I always adjust an image. Second, that iPhone image is a bit more 'natural' if we all wanted that, there'd be no need for OLED TVs. That extra punch the other two phones start with, and it really isn't that much, means most people get a great shot they can share. I've noticed the iPhone's slight red bias. Noticeable as you point out in skin tones. Ummmm. Might just be something that happened. But it could be a trick Playboy photographers used to use (in like the 1960s and 70s). They used a red enhancing filter, that isn't actually red. Also the difference between Kodachrome and Ektachrome, back in the day, was about +3-4CCs of red. (But it doesn't make Ektachrome look like Kodachrome, just a bit closer.) I kind of don't get the adjustable aperture in the iPhone. These lenses have such a short focal length that the added depth of field is pretty meaningless. And the sensors have such a large range that it's also not needed. (Shooting slide film back in the day, if anything was 4.5 stops below exposure -- it was textureless black, the other way, pure white. Slide film had a range of about 7 stops. My D850 has a range of at least 15 stops. These phones somewhere in between.) My biggest issue with the iPhone camera is not image quality, it's all the nonsense trying to take the photo. Just selecting Camera on my iPhone, even with the side button is not just one or two steps, it's contextual to what State the phone is in. Did I go from sleep to Camera? Then when I go out of camera to Photos, I have to unlock the phone. I might not have this right, but it always seems to be different. Total pain. I've spent months swearing I will never buy another iPhone so long as that stupid Live button is dead center on the screen when that menu pops up (a menu 95% of the time I don't want.) A Live image takes up 3xs the space as a regular image, so I have to make a Duplicate (not live) then delete the Live one. A woman at Dodger Stadium took a half dozen photos of my girlfriend and me, inadvertently hitting the stupid Live button. I then had to spend 20 minutes deleting them, all the time wondering why didn't the iPhone camera see that flash fill was needed? This is just so typical. The thing you could use is never automatic, or even offered or suggested; the thing you were sick to death of the day after it was first introduced? It's forever and as often as Apple can trick you into turning it on. (And don't expect them to fix it. On their computer keyboards they still have the utterly useless Caps Lock key. You can turn it off, but the one thing you could use it for, a Shift Key - you can't reassign it to. I have plastic and Popsicle stick pieces taped to my Shift Key so I can use that space for something. Plus ça change, plus la même choses. )
